title: EAU Management of Non-neurogenic Male LUTS 2026: Diagnostic Evaluation (4.12 Urodynamics)
scope: Supports the selective indications for pressure-flow studies before invasive treatment (Qmax above 10 ml/s, voided volume below 150 ml, age below 50 or above 80, failed previous invasive treatment), the BOOI and BCI formulas and cut-offs, and the UPSTREAM results.

title: EAU Management of Non-neurogenic Male LUTS 2026: Disease Management
scope: Supports avoiding antimuscarinics when the post-void residual exceeds 150 ml, the urodynamic safety of beta-3 agonists in men with obstruction, and counselling about ejaculatory dysfunction with selective alpha-blockers, which is more frequent in younger men.

title: Bladder outlet obstruction index, bladder contractility index and bladder voiding efficiency (BJU International, 1999)
scope: Original description of the BOOI and BCI used to classify male pressure-flow studies.

title: UPSTREAM: noninferiority randomised trial of urodynamics before prostate surgery in 26 hospitals (European Urology, 2020)
scope: Supports that routine urodynamics did not significantly reduce surgery (38% vs 36%) and was non-inferior for symptoms.

title: Preoperative detrusor underactivity and transurethral surgery for BPH: systematic review and meta-analysis (Journal of Urology, 2018)
scope: Supports smaller symptom and flow improvements after transurethral surgery when detrusor underactivity is present before surgery.

title: Urodynamics and safety of mirabegron in men with LUTS and bladder outlet obstruction (Journal of Urology, 2013)
scope: Supports that mirabegron did not adversely affect Qmax or PdetQmax versus placebo after 12 weeks in 200 men with LUTS and obstruction.

title: Primary bladder neck obstruction in young adult men: systematic review and meta-analysis (Urology Research and Practice, 2024)
scope: Supports short-term benefit of alpha-blockers and stronger long-term improvement after bladder neck incision in men aged 18 to 50.

title: Primary bladder neck obstruction and dysfunctional voiding in young men: systematic review and meta-analysis (European Urology Focus, 2025)
scope: Supports video-urodynamics as the diagnostic standard, alpha-blockers first and bladder neck incision after failure, ejaculatory dysfunction in 47–50% with alpha-blockers, and shared decision-making given low-quality evidence.

title: Ejaculatory disorder with silodosin in the treatment of prostatic hyperplasia (BMC Urology, 2012)
scope: Supports that ejaculatory function returned in all affected men after the alpha-blocker was stopped.

title: EAU Neuro-Urology 2026: The Guideline
scope: Supports physiological filling rates and same-session repeat measurements, video-urodynamics in neurological patients, upper tract risk from high filling pressures, augmentation for low compliance after failed less invasive treatment, and caution with prostate surgery in neurological disease. Also supports blood pressure and heart rate monitoring during urodynamics in patients at risk of autonomic dysreflexia (lesions at or above T6; systolic rise above 20 mmHg), antimuscarinics first line for neurogenic detrusor overactivity, botulinum toxin when they are ineffective, no beta-3 agonists to reduce urodynamic overactivity (mirabegron does not improve urodynamic parameters in neurogenic detrusor overactivity), intermittent catheterisation four to six times a day with volumes generally not above 400–500 ml (in aseptic catheterisation, five times a day reduced urinary infections), that reflex triggering can provoke dysreflexia and that assisted emptying needs low outlet resistance.

title: Video-urodynamic and sphincter motor unit potential analyses in Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy (Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry, 2001)
scope: Supports an open bladder neck at the start of filling (53% vs 0%), a residual above 100 ml and neurogenic sphincter potentials (93% vs 5%) as features of MSA rather than Parkinson's disease.

title: How to recognise patients with parkinsonism who should not have urological surgery (British Journal of Urology, 1997)
scope: Supports that all 11 men with MSA who had TURP were incontinent afterwards and lists the urogenital warning signs of MSA.

title: Movement Disorder Society criteria for the diagnosis of multiple system atrophy (Movement Disorders, 2022)
scope: Supports unexplained voiding difficulty with a residual above 100 ml, urgency incontinence and neurogenic orthostatic hypotension as autonomic criteria.

title: EAU Pocket Guidelines: Non-neurogenic Female LUTS 2026
scope: Supports female BOO work-up with video-urodynamics and urethrocystoscopy, sling revision rather than dilatation or urethrotomy after midurethral tapes (theoretical risk of mesh extrusion), intermittent catheterisation and sacral nerve stimulation for underactive bladder and functional obstruction, alpha-blockers only off-label and no routine parasympathomimetics, and the prolapse reduction test with counselling about combined surgery. Also supports onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U for refractory OAB or urgency incontinence with counselling about infection and catheterisation, bladder training and drugs for urgency incontinence, treating the most bothersome component of mixed incontinence first with a warning that surgery is less successful than in pure stress incontinence, a shared choice between midurethral sling, colposuspension, autologous sling and less effective bulking agents for stress incontinence, not using urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure to grade severity, and warning women who strain to empty about prolapse. Further: supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months as first-line therapy for stress or mixed incontinence (strong), caution with long-term anticholinergics in elderly women and assessment of the anticholinergic burden (strong), and no consistent evidence that preoperative detrusor overactivity is associated with failure of midurethral slings (LE 3).

title: EAU Non-neurogenic Female LUTS 2026: Diagnosis
scope: Supports that there is no universally accepted urodynamic threshold for BOO in women and that pressure-flow studies separate BOO from detrusor underactivity. Also supports urodynamics when findings may change invasive treatment or the diagnosis is uncertain, that a urodynamic diagnosis of detrusor overactivity does not influence treatment outcomes in OAB, and monitoring the post-void residual during treatments that may impair emptying.

title: EAU Non-neurogenic Female LUTS 2026: Disease Management
scope: Related management chapter for female voiding dysfunction, underactive bladder and prolapse with LUTS. States that identifying detrusor overactivity on urodynamics does not appear to influence the outcome of onabotulinumtoxinA in urgency incontinence and recommends bladder training, antimuscarinics and beta-3 agonists for OAB.

title: A nomogram for diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction in women (Neurourology and Urodynamics, 2018; journal review)
scope: Supports the female BOO index (PdetQmax − 2.2 × Qmax): below 0 under 10%, above 5 about 50% and above 18 over 90% probability of obstruction.

title: Sacral neuromodulation for women with Fowler's syndrome (European Urology, 2000)
scope: Supports sacral neuromodulation as the treatment that can restore voiding in women with Fowler's syndrome.

title: OPUS: a midurethral sling to reduce incontinence after vaginal prolapse repair (New England Journal of Medicine, 2012)
scope: Supports incontinence at 12 months of 27.3% with versus 43.0% without a prophylactic sling in all continent women (NNT 6.3), a larger 3-month difference after a positive prolapse reduction test (29.6% vs 71.9%) without a significant interaction, and more bladder perforation, infection, bleeding and incomplete emptying.

title: ICS abstract: bladder compliance – a review of practice
scope: Supports that there are no agreed normal values or thresholds for compliance and that higher filling rates reduce compliance.

title: ICS teaching module: evaluating and reporting a urodynamic test (based on ICS Good Urodynamic Practices 2016)
scope: Supports quality control of urodynamic traces: cough pressure transmission, continuous filling and recognising rectal contractions.

title: ICS workshop: basic urodynamics (Good Urodynamic Practices)
scope: Supports resting pressure ranges by position and flushing a line when one cough peak is less than 70% of the other.

title: Urodynamic quality assessment and artefact recognition (teaching slides)
scope: Supports the pattern of rectal contractions (Pabd rises without Pves, so Pdet falls), cough tests every minute or 50 ml and immediately before and after voiding, the 70% transmission rule, flushing the line when a cough response is too small, and that an expelled catheter drops Pves, usually to well below zero, with no response to cough checks.

title: IUGA: troubleshooting in urodynamics – technical
scope: Supports flushing air bubbles, checking connections and repositioning catheters when pressure transmission is poor.

title: ICCS standardisation of terminology of lower urinary tract function in children and adolescents (2016 update)
scope: Supports the definitions of dysfunctional voiding and flow-curve shapes, the 50% expected-capacity rule for valid uroflowmetry and age-specific residual thresholds.

title: EAU Pocket Guidelines: Non-neurogenic Male LUTS 2026
scope: Supports a bladder diary for at least three days to assess male LUTS, particularly nocturia (strong), treating the underlying causes of nocturia (strong), urodynamics before further invasive treatment after an unsuccessful invasive treatment (weak), and urodynamics when surgery is considered in men with bothersome, predominantly voiding LUTS and Qmax above 10 ml/s (weak).

title: ICS Good Urodynamic Practices and Terms 2016: uroflowmetry, cystometry and pressure-flow study
scope: Supports that an expelled catheter shows as a sudden drop in Pves or Pabd, usually below zero, and should prompt correction or repetition; repeating a test after technical errors or artefacts but not routinely after an adequate test; reporting the provocation and recording site of a leak point pressure; cough-associated detrusor overactivity as overactivity starting immediately after a cough; the leak point pressure as the pressure at the moment leakage becomes visible; the inevitable delay between pressure and flow signals, to be corrected for in pressure-flow analysis; and a cough check of the catheter position after pressure-flow.

title: IUGA/ICS joint report on the terminology for female pelvic floor dysfunction (2010; reprint)
scope: Supports normal (previously 'stable') detrusor function, increased bladder sensation during filling cystometry, compliance as volume change over detrusor pressure change without defined normal categories, mixed urinary incontinence as a symptom (leakage with urgency and with effort, sneezing or coughing) and urodynamic stress incontinence as leakage with raised abdominal pressure without a detrusor contraction.

title: ICS terminology discussion: reduced and absent bladder sensation
scope: Supports the categories of bladder sensation during filling cystometry: normal (increasing sensation up to a strong desire to void), reduced and absent.

title: Autonomic dysreflexia (CMAJ, 2012)
scope: Supports autonomic dysreflexia after injuries above T6 with a sudden blood pressure rise, reflex bradycardia, headache and sweating, and its acute management: sit upright, loosen clothing, monitor blood pressure, check and empty the bladder first, and a short-acting antihypertensive if systolic pressure stays above 150 mmHg.

title: CAN-SCIP: autonomic dysreflexia during cystoscopic and urodynamic procedures (PVA 2020)
scope: Supports blood pressure monitoring at least every 2 minutes during urological procedures in people at risk, draining the bladder first, and ending the procedure and sitting the patient up when dysreflexia is not controlled.

title: EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures 2026 (full text)
scope: Supports a reduced maximum flow with a prolonged plateau as characteristic of constrictive obstruction, that the flow pattern is not a reliable screening tool for stricture, uroflowmetry with post-void residual (strong), and retrograde urethrography for location and length, combined with voiding cystourethrography for (nearly) obliterative strictures (strong).

title: EAU Pocket Guidelines: Urethral Strictures 2026
scope: Supports urethrotomy or dilatation for a primary, single, short (below 2 cm), non-obliterative bulbar stricture (weak), no more than two urethrotomies or dilatations when urethroplasty is a viable option (strong), no urethrotomy for penile strictures and no permanent urethral stents (strong).

title: ICCS report: management of dysfunctional voiding in children (Journal of Urology, 2010)
scope: Supports repeated uroflowmetry with EMG, urotherapy and constipation treatment first, biofeedback as a later step, and invasive studies only for refractory cases.
